content.rendered:
The olive grove at Gethsemane. Past midnight. Jesus knowing exactly what the next twelve hours would hold. He fell on His face and prayed the prayer that holds the entire New Testament doctrine of submission in a single sentence. “Not My will, but Yours be done.”

The Gospel For Today | Thursday, October 15, 2026 | Teach Me How to Pray, Day 13

Today’s Scripture

“He went a little farther and fell on His face, and prayed, saying, ‘O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.'”
Matthew 26:39 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

In an olive grove on the western slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, Jesus went to pray late on Thursday night. The grove was called Gethsemane, which means “oil press.” It was the kind of place where ripe olives were crushed under heavy stones to release their oil. The symbolism was not accidental. Jesus went to a place of crushing, knowing exactly what the next twelve hours would hold. The arrest. The illegal trials. The scourging. The crown of thorns. The nails. The cross. The cup of the wrath of God poured out on Him for the sin of the world. He took Peter, James, and John with Him deeper into the grove, told them to watch and pray, and then went a little further on His own. Luke tells us His sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground. Mark tells us He was greatly amazed and deeply distressed. And then He fell on His face and prayed the prayer that is the hinge of the whole New Testament doctrine of submission.

Twelve days ago we began this series with Jesus praying before daylight in Mark 1:35. We studied the authority He walked in, the mountains He moved, the storms He stilled, the dead He raised. And now, at the climax of the series, we must see the other side of the pattern. Authority always travels with submission. The same Jesus who said “Lazarus, come forth!” and “Peace, be still!” is the Jesus who said in Gethsemane, “Not as I will, but as You will.” He was fully God, fully Man, and fully submitted. His will was not in conflict with the Father’s. It was aligned with the Father’s. And in the hour when every fibre of His humanity recoiled from what was ahead, He prayed the prayer that confirmed the alignment one final time.

The Passion Translation renders Gethsemane with searching tenderness: “Then he walked a short distance away, and overcome with grief, he threw himself facedown on the ground. He prayed that if it were possible, he would not have to experience this hour of suffering. He prayed, ‘Abba, my Father, all things are possible for you. Please,take this cup of suffering away from me! Yet what I want is not important, for I only desire to fulfil your plan for me'” (Mark 14:35-36 TPT). The Amplified Bible Classic Edition adds: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from Me; nevertheless, not what I will [not what I desire], but as You will and desire” (Matthew 26:39 AMPC). Not what I desire. The honesty of the request is honoured. The submission that follows is total.

How Jesus Prayed

The Format. Honest request followed by complete submission. Jesus did not pretend He wanted the cross. He asked, if possible, for the cup to pass. The honesty was not a lack of faith. It was reverent transparency before the Father. And it was immediately followed by the sentence that put the Father’s will above His own.

The Essence. This is the Son submitting to the Father in the hardest moment of His earthly life. The believer sees that submission in prayer is not weakness. It is the mature trust of a child who knows the Father’s wisdom is higher than the child’s preference, especially when the preference is understandable, legitimate, and human.

The Authority. Here is the paradox of New Testament authority. The believer walks in Kingdom authority precisely to the degree the believer is submitted to Kingdom will. The authority Jesus wielded over demons, sickness, and death flowed from a life that was continually saying to the Father, “not My will, but Yours.” Unsubmitted authority is not Kingdom authority. It is self-will dressed up in religious vocabulary. The believer who insists on their own agenda cannot carry the authority of One who gave up His.

The Assurance. Even in the deepest distress of Gethsemane, Jesus addressed the Father as Abba. The intimacy was unbroken. The relationship was secure. The Father was still Father. The believer may bring the hardest, most honest requests into prayer without any threat to the relationship. The Father can be trusted with the honest cry.

The Submission. “Not as I will, but as You will.” This is the sentence that unlocks every other sentence Jesus ever prayed. Every mountain-moving declaration, every healing command, every dead-rising word, flowed from a will continually aligned with the Father’s. Submission is the river bed in which the water of authority flows. Take away the bed, and the water scatters into mud.

The Result. Jesus rose from Gethsemane settled. When the arresting party arrived with Judas at the head, Jesus met them with such presence that they fell backward to the ground. The settled Son walked to the cross because the submitted Son had risen from His knees with the Father’s will as His only agenda. For Gospelbuzz readers today, wherever you are reading this from, in Lagos or London or Manila or Nairobi or Sao Paulo, is there a cup you have been asking the Father to take away? A trial. A season. An assignment you did not choose. A loss you cannot undo. Bring the honest request. Then pray the sentence that closed the door on all second-guessing in the heart of Jesus. Not my will, Father. Yours.

Prayer (Pattern After Jesus)

Address. Abba, Father. I come to You with the honest cry of my heart. You are my Father. I am Your child. The relationship is secure, whatever is in the cup.

Honest Request. If it is possible, Father, [name the specific thing you would ask Him to remove, change, or take away]. You know my heart. You know what I would prefer. I bring it to You openly.

Submission. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will. Your wisdom is higher than mine. Your purposes are better than mine. Your timing is wiser than mine. I surrender my preference to Your plan.

Confirmation. Whatever Your will is in this matter, strengthen me to walk in it. Give me the grace Jesus received in Gethsemane. Let me rise from my knees settled.

In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

I pray with the authority of the Son who submitted in Gethsemane. My will is aligned with the Father’s. My preferences are surrendered to His wisdom. The river of Kingdom authority flows through the river bed of Kingdom submission in my life.
